title: Better together
description: Discover why the mix changes the risk.

questions.prompt: What does a 50/50 portfolio return in a recession?
questions.context: Invest half your starting wealth in each stock. These are one-period returns; ignore fees.
questions.explanation: The portfolio returns 10%: half of −20% plus half of 40%.
questions.detail: Use initial wealth weights: \(R_p=0.5(-20\%)+0.5(40\%)=10\%\). In the boom the returns swap, so the portfolio again earns 10%. Perfect offsetting eliminates risk in this stylized two-state example. Real assets generally share shocks and do not offset perfectly.
questions.misconception: Adding −20% and 40% without weights gives 20%, but you did not invest all your wealth in each stock.

questions.prompt: Owning exactly 30 stocks guarantees that all investment risk is eliminated.
questions.explanation: False. There is no magic stock count, and systematic risk can remain.
questions.detail: The lecture’s stock-count curve illustrates diminishing benefits from adding holdings. The benefit depends on weights and co-movement. Thirty nearly identical exposures can remain concentrated; thirty different exposures still need not eliminate market risk.
questions.misconception: A rule of thumb about reducing firm-specific risk is not a guarantee about every portfolio.

source.section: The 30-Stock Curve: Watching Idiosyncratic Risk Vanish

questions.prompt: Match each pattern to its meaning.

pairs.right: Returns tend to move in the same direction.
Returns tend to move in opposite directions.
No linear co-movement; dependence can still exist.
The portfolio earns 10% in either state.

questions.explanation: Diversification depends on co-movement, not just the risk of each holding.
questions.detail: Positive correlation means returns tend to move together; negative correlation means they tend to move oppositely. Zero correlation means no linear relationship, not necessarily independence. Exact risk elimination requires special weights and return patterns, as in the lecture’s two-state example.
questions.misconception: Negative correlation helps diversification, but does not by itself guarantee a risk-free portfolio.

questions.prompt: Leo owns ten airline stocks. Why might this portfolio still be concentrated?

options.text: Many holdings share fuel-cost and travel-demand exposure.
Ten stocks always have exactly ten times one stock’s risk.
Different company names guarantee independent returns.
Diversification only works with large dollar investments.

questions.explanation: Different names can share the same underlying economic drivers.
questions.detail: A fuel-price increase or collapse in travel demand may affect many airlines together. Adding more airline names can reduce some firm-specific exposure while leaving industry concentration. Broader economic exposures matter more than simply counting ticker symbols.
questions.misconception: Owning more securities is not the same as owning different sources of risk.

questions.prompt: Put this exposure-based portfolio review in order.

items.text: List your holdings and other income sources.
Identify the economic drivers shared by those exposures.
Compare additions that reduce the identified overlap.
Check the combined portfolio’s remaining risks.

questions.explanation: Start with what you own, find overlap, compare changes, then assess the whole mix.
questions.detail: This is an educational review workflow: first map existing exposure, including labor income. Identify common shocks before comparing additions. Finally assess the combined portfolio; an asset’s risk in isolation cannot tell you everything about its contribution to the mix.
questions.misconception: Picking the individually least volatile asset without considering the existing portfolio can miss valuable hedging relationships.

source.section: The Double-Whammy Risk; Fallacy 2: The Illusion of Diversification
